blocks.text: Inflammation is one of the most general non-specific responses to infection. Infected or injured cells release chemical signals such as histamine and prostaglandins, which widen the local blood vessels and increase capillary blood flow at the site; the capillaries also become more permeable. The result is redness, swelling and warmth: inflammation. The heat makes the site unfavourable for microbial growth, promotes healing and increases the mobility of white blood cells.

blocks.alt: A cut in the skin surface lets microbes in. Injured cells nearby release orange dots of histamine and prostaglandins. Below, a widened red capillary leaks fluid upward, and white phagocytes squeeze out of it towards the microbes. A note gives the signs: redness, swelling and warmth.
blocks.caption: The inflammatory response (original diagram after Figure 21.9).
blocks.long_description: Infected or injured cells release chemical signals such as histamine and prostaglandins. These widen the local blood vessels, increasing capillary blood flow, and make the capillaries more permeable, giving redness, swelling and warmth: inflammation. The heat makes the site unfavourable for microbes, promotes healing and increases the movement of white cells. More phagocytes, macrophages and neutrophils, leave the blood for the inflamed tissue and engulf microbes; monocytes arrive and release chemicals, and macrophages clean up dead microbes, cells and debris.

blocks.text: More phagocytes, macrophages and neutrophils, migrate from the blood into the inflamed tissue and engulf microbes. Monocytes arrive and release chemicals to kill microbes, and macrophages then clean up dead microbes, cells and debris. The inflammatory response is often strong enough to stop the spread of microbes.

blocks.title: For information
blocks.text: The pus of some infections is a mixture of dead or dying neutrophils, broken-down tissue cells and dead pathogens. In some cases, for example arthritis, inflammation occurs without infection or injury: a misdirected immune response.
